The Keeper's Ledgers
The ferry to Carrow Island ran twice a day
in summer and, after the first week of
October, only when the harbormaster felt
like it. Nora Pell took the 7:40 crossing on a
Tuesday, with one suitcase, a borrowed
raincoat and a letter from a solicitor she
had never met.
The letter was short. Her great-uncle,
Edmund Pell, had died in March at the age
of 91. He had left her the keeper's cottage at
Carrow Light, its contents, and "such pa-
pers as may be found therein." There was
no money to speak of. There was, the solici-
tor added, a small matter of unpaid harbor
dues amounting to £38.
She had met Edmund exactly once, at a
wedding in 1987, when she was nine. He
had given her a brass button and told her it
came from the coat of a drowned captain.
Her mother said afterwards that he had
bought a bag of them in a market in Hull.
The crossing took fifty minutes. A man
in a yellow jacket checked her ticket twice,
the second time apparently for something
to do. "You'll be the niece," he said. "Great-
niece," said Nora. He nodded as though
this confirmed a rumor. "He kept the
books, you know. Right up to the end."
"What books?"
"The light's books. Every ship, every
night." He looked out at the water. "No-
body asked him to. The light's been auto-
matic since 1994."
The cottage stood about two hundred
yards from the tower, behind a wall that
had been repaired so many times it was
mostly mortar. The key was under a flower-
pot, which the solicitor's letter had de-
scribed, with evident disapproval, as "the
customary arrangement."
Inside, it smelled of paraffin and old pa-
per. There were two rooms downstairs and
one above. Every wall that did not hold a
window held a shelf, and every shelf held
ledgers: tall, narrow, bound in green cloth,
their spines numbered in white ink. She
counted 112 of them before she gave up.
She took down the nearest one. The first
page was dated 3 January 1961. Below the
date, in a small upright hand, her great-un-
cle had written the time, the wind, the state
of the sea, and then a list of every vessel
that had passed the light between dusk and
dawn. There were eleven that night. He had
noted the name of each one where he could
read it, and where he could not he had writ-
ten "unknown, two masts" or "unknown,
coaster, heading north."
The next page was 4 January, and the
page after that was the 5th. She turned to
the middle of the book and then to the end.
He had not missed a night.
